question:
An internal auditor at a US bank finds that the FX desk prices all strikes of one-month EUR/USD options at a single implied volatility equal to the current at-the-money implied volatility, while the market quotes the usual foreign currency smile. Which of the following findings is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “lognormal” means a lognormal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation as the implied distribution, rates are continuously compounded, and all options are European.

options.A: The practice is harmless, because put-call parity holds for any distribution and so keeps the desk’s prices consistent with the market at every strike.
options.B: The practice is equivalent to assuming a lognormal distribution; it understates the probability of extreme moves and so underprices deep out-of-the-money options in both wings.
options.C: The practice is equivalent to assuming a lognormal distribution; it overstates the probability of extreme moves and so overprices deep out-of-the-money options in both wings.
options.D: The practice is equivalent to using the market’s implied distribution, provided the at-the-money volatility is taken from current market prices.

solution:
**One volatility for every strike**

Stem in one line: an FX desk prices all EUR/USD strikes at the at-the-money volatility while the market shows a smile; what is the finding?

**Concept and theory**

GARP Summary: “The Black-Scholes-Merton model and its extensions assume that the probability distribution of the underlying asset at any given future time is lognormal. This assumption is not the one made by traders.” For exchange rates, traders assume a distribution with “a heavier right tail and a heavier left tail than the lognormal distribution”, and “Traders use volatility smiles to allow for nonlognormality.” A single volatility across all strikes is the lognormal assumption itself: one $\sigma$ fixes one lognormal distribution, and that distribution reproduces BSM prices at every strike. A flat implied volatility curve and a lognormal implied distribution are two descriptions of the same thing.

**Applying it to this question**

The desk’s flat volatility equals the bottom of the market’s U-shaped curve. It therefore assumes lognormal tails, which are thinner than the market’s implied tails in both directions. Too little probability of extreme moves ⇒ deep out-of-the-money calls and puts priced below market ⇒ both wings underpriced.

solution:
**What equity and currency traders assume**

Stem in one line: which statement comparing equity and currency option pricing with the lognormal is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

Schweser’s key concept for LO 17.c is a two-line summary of the whole LO: “Currency traders believe there is a greater chance of extreme price movements than predicted by a lognormal distribution. Equity traders believe the probability of large down movements in price is greater than large up movements in price, as compared with a lognormal distribution.” GARP’s Summary says the same: traders “assume the probability distribution of an equity price has a heavier left tail and a less heavy right tail than the lognormal distribution. They also assume that the probability distribution of an exchange rate has a heavier right tail and a heavier left tail.”

| Market | Implied distribution vs lognormal | Smile shape |
|---|---|---|
| Equity | Heavier left, less heavy right | Downward-sloping skew |

solution:
**Equity versus currency smiles: what is not correct**

Stem in one line: which statement in a EUR client brochure comparing equity and currency smiles is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Summary puts the two patterns side by side. For equity options the smile tends to be downward sloping: out-of-the-money puts and in-the-money calls (low strikes) have high implied volatilities; out-of-the-money calls and in-the-money puts (high strikes) have low ones. For foreign currency options the smile is U-shaped: both out-of-the-money and in-the-money options have higher implied volatilities than at-the-money options.

GARP 17.3 adds two facts about the equity pattern: it applies to options on individual stocks and on stock indices, and it has existed only since the crash of October 1987. Before that crash there was no marked volatility smile for equity options; implied volatilities were much less dependent on strike price (Business Snapshot 17.2). That history is what motivates the crashophobia explanation.

A: deep out-of-the-money put (low strike) above deep out-of-the-money call (high strike). Correct. B: the currency U-shape. Correct. C: GARP 17.3 says “both on individual stocks and on stock indices”. Correct. D: claims a marked pre-1987 skew. Not correct.

solution:
**Weakness of plotting the smile against strike**

Stem in one line: what is wrong with storing an index option smile as implied volatility against $K$ after the index has risen 6%?

**Concept and theory**

A volatility smile is a plot of the Black-Scholes-Merton implied volatility of options with the same maturity against some measure of where the strike sits. The vertical axis is always implied volatility; the question this LO asks is what to put on the horizontal axis. GARP §17.4 lists the choices in order of refinement:

| Horizontal axis | At-the-money point | Reason or weakness (GARP) |
|---|---|---|
| Strike $K$ | $K$ = $S_{0}$ | Depends on the asset price: curve moves right (left) as the price rises (falls) |
| $K/S_{0}$ | $K/S_{0}$ = 1 | Removes that dependence; used for Figures 17.1 and 17.3 |
| $K/F_{0}$ | $K$ = $F_{0}$ | Refinement: $F_{0}$ is the risk-neutral expected price at the option’s maturity |
| Delta | call 0.5, put −0.5 | Sometimes extends smiles beyond European and American calls and puts |

The pattern of implied volatility is organised around the at-the-money option (for currencies, lowest at the money and rising either side; for equities, falling as strike rises). **Re-mapping a $K/S_{0}$ smile onto strikes after a move**

**Concept and theory**

If a smile is stable when written as $\sigma_{\text{imp}}$ = $f$ ($K/S_{0}$), then a given implied volatility belongs to a given moneyness $K/S_{0}$, not to a given strike. When $S_{0}$ changes, each point on the curve against $K$ moves to a new strike so that $K/S_{0}$ is preserved:

$K_{\text{new}}$ = $\left( \frac{K}{S_{0}} \right) \times S_{0,\text{new}}$

where $K$ is the strike, $S_{0}$ the current asset price (here the exchange rate in JPY per USD), and $S_{0,\text{new}}$ today’s rate. This is the quantitative form of GARP’s statement that the curve against $K$ moves right when the price rises: the shift is proportional (every strike is scaled by $S_{0,\text{new}}/S_{0}$), not a fixed number of yen. The at-the-money point is $K/S_{0}$ = 1, so it sits at the current rate.
